dervis-irab:1-11.t:
* Vocabulary:
(سَجى): its darkness grew still and settled. In al-Mukhtār: "Al-shayʾ sajā (from the pattern samā) means it became still and lasted. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذا سَجى﴾ means: it lasted and became still. From it come al-baḥr al-sājī (the calm sea) and ṭarf sājin (a still gaze). And sajjā al-mayyit tasjiyatan means: he spread a garment over him." The poet said:
يا حبذا القمراء والليل الساج ... وطرق مثل ملاء النسّاج
(How dear is the moonlit night and the still night, and paths like the weaver's cloaks.)
Al-sāj also means the green ṭaylasān (shawl); its plural is sīyān. More on it will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(وَدَّعَكَ): The majority read it with shadda on the dāl (wadda'aka), from tawdīʿ, which is an intensive form of wadʿ, because whoever bids you farewell, leaving, has gone to the extreme in abandoning you. It is reported that revelation was delayed from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for some days, so the polytheists said: "Muhammad's Lord has bid him farewell and hated him." It is also said that Umm Jamīl, the wife of Abū Lahab, said to him: "O Muhammad, I see nothing but that your devil has abandoned you," and so the sūra was revealed. It was also read with a light dāl (wadaʿaka), from their saying wadaʿahu, meaning "he left him." There is disagreement over daʿ, meaning "leave": is it conjugated, so that the past tense, verbal noun, active participle and passive participle are formed from it? Al-Jawharī said: its past tense has been left obsolete (umīta). Others said: it may occur out of poetic necessity, and this is the well-known view; yet it occurs in the Qur'an, ﴿ما وَدَّعَكَ﴾, and in the hadith: "Let people stop their abandoning (wadʿihim) of the Friday prayers, or Allah will surely seal their hearts, and then they will surely be among the heedless," meaning their leaving them. The passive participle and other forms have also occurred in poetry, so it is permissible to say that it is rarely used, not that it is obsolete. The poet said:
ليت شعري عن خليلي ما الذي ... غاله في الحب حتى ودعه
(Would that I knew about my friend: what was it that destroyed him in love, until he left it?)
(قَلى): he hated. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Qalaytuhu qalyan and qalawtuhu qalwan (from the patterns ḍaraba and qatala) is the roasting in the maqlā, which is a mif'al with kasra; it is sometimes said maqlāh with the tāʾ marbūṭa. Meat and the like is maqlī with yāʾ and maqlū with wāw. The one who does it is qallāʾ with shadda, because it is a trade like ʿaṭṭār and najjār. And qalaytu al-rajul aqlīhi (from the pattern ramā), qilan with kasra and shortened, and sometimes lengthened, when I hated him; and from the pattern taʿiba it is a dialectal variant." And in a hadith from ʿĀʾisha, a man asked permission to see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Let him in, for he is a bad man of his clan." When he entered, he spoke gently to him. ʿĀʾisha said: "O Messenger of Allah, you said to him what you said, and when he entered you spoke gently to him?" He said: "O ʿĀʾisha, the worst of people in standing on the Day of Resurrection is the one whom people abandoned, or left, to guard against his obscenity."
Ibn Khālawayh said: "One says qalāhu yaqlāhu, with fatḥa on both the past and the imperfect. In the speech of the Arabs there is no verb with fatḥa on both the past and imperfect that does not contain a guttural letter, except qalā yaqlā, jabā yajbā, salā yaslā, abā yabā, ghasā yaghsā and rakina yarkanu, on the authority of al-Shaybānī. As for their saying qulūb al-busr wa-l-sawīq, it is with wāw, and the verbal noun is al-qalw; and al-qalw is the donkey." Perhaps al-Shaybānī's report, on which Ibn Khālawayh relied, is something peculiar to him, since in all the lexicons we have only what the author of al-Miṣbāḥ cited has come down. The text of al-Tāj: ...that qalāhu in the sense of hatred is like raḍiyahu yarḍāhu. And in the hadith: "I found people: akhbir taqlih" (test them and you will hate them), with the hāʾ as a pausal hāʾ, its form being the form of an imperative but its meaning being about people, that is: whoever tests them will hate them. The meaning is: I found people about whom this saying is said.
(فَآوى): The majority read āwā with an alif after the hamza, a four-letter verb, from āwāhu yuʾwīhi. Abū al-Ashhab read fa-awā as a three-letter verb. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Awā ilā manzilihi yaʾwī (from the pattern ḍaraba), awyan: he stayed. Sometimes it is made transitive by itself, so it is said awā manzilahu. Al-maʾwā, with fatḥa on the wāw, is the dwelling of every animal. Āwaytu Zaydan, with the long vowel, in the transitive. Some make it a verb used both intransitively and transitively, saying awaytuhu on the pattern of ḍarabtuhu; and some also use the four-letter form intransitively, but a group rejected that."
(عائِلًا): poor, and this is the reading of the majority. One says ʿāla Zaydun (from the pattern sāra) meaning he became poor, and aʿāla when his dependents became many. It was also read ʿayyilan, with kasra on the doubled yāʾ, like sayyid. This root has two origins, one with wāw and one with yāʾ. As for the wāw one, al-Qāmūs says of it:
"ʿāla: that is, he wronged and deviated from the truth; and the scale: it fell short, and he cheated or added, yaʿūlu and yaʿīlu; and their affair became severe and grave; and the thing overcame so-and-so, weighed on him and concerned him; and the inheritance share in arithmetic increased and rose, and I made it increase (ʿiltuhā) and aʿltuhā; and ʿāla so-and-so ʿawlan and ʿiyālatan: his dependents became many, like aʿwala and aʿyala; and ʿiyālahu ʿawlan, ʿuʾūlan and ʿiyālatan: he sufficed them and supplied them, like aʿālahum and ʿayyalahum; and aʿwala: he raised his voice in weeping and shouting, like ʿawwala. The noun is al-ʿawl, al-ʿawla and al-ʿawīl; and ʿalayhi adalla and ḥamala, like ʿawwala; and so-and-so was eager, like aʿāla and aʿyala; and the bow twanged; and ʿīla ʿawluhu: his mother bereaved him; and my patience was overcome, so he is muʿwal, like ʿāl in both; and ʿīla mā huwa ʿāʾiluhu: what he is to overcome was overcome (said of one whose speech and the like is wondered at); and al-ʿawl is everything that burdens you, and that by which help is sought, and the sustenance of dependents; and ʿawwala ʿalayhi mu'awwalan: he relied and depended, and the noun is like ʿinab; and ʿayyiluka, like kayyis and kitāb: those whom you support; and its wāw is a yāʾ, and the plural is ʿālatun." Its commentator added: "Al-Ṣāghānī said in al-Takmila: al-ʿiyāl is the plural of ʿayyil, like jiyād, plural of jayyid; it is the one whose maintenance is obligatory upon one, and it can be a noun for a single person, as al-Ḥarīrī mentioned in his Maqāmāt and al-Muṭarrizī mentioned in his commentary."
[Translator's note: the Arabic text of this quotation from al-Qāmūs is somewhat garbled in the printed source, and the translation follows it as written.]
As for the yāʾ one, the author of al-Qāmūs said: "ʿāla yaʿīlu ʿaylan, ʿaylatan, ʿuyūlan and maʿīlan: he became poor, so he is ʿāʾil, and the plural is ʿālatun, ʿayyil and ʿaylā like sakrā. The noun is al-ʿayla. And al-miʿyal is the lion, the leopard and the wolf, because it yaʿīlu ṣaydan, i.e. seeks prey. And ʿālanī al-shayʾ ʿaylan and maʿīlan: it left me in need. And in his walk: he swayed, strutted and swaggered, like taʿayyala," to the end of what is given under this root.

* I'rab:
(وَالضُّحى وَاللَّيْلِ إِذا سَجى ما وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ وَما قَلى): The wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; (الضُّحى) is genitive by the wāw of oath, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted verb of the oath. (اللَّيْلِ) is conjoined to (الضُّحى). Ibn Hishām allowed the wāw in (وَاللَّيْلِ) to be either a conjunction or an oath wāw. He said: "The correct view is the first; otherwise each would need a response." (إِذا) is an adverb of mere time, attached to the verb of the oath; parallels have been given before. The clause (سَجى) is in the position of a genitive, through the annexation of the adverb to it. (ما) is a negative particle, and it is the response to the oath, and the clause has no grammatical position. (وَدَّعَكَ) is a past verb with its direct object, and (رَبُّكَ) is the agent. (وَما قَلى) is conjoined to (ما وَدَّعَكَ).
(وَلَلْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لَكَ مِنَ الْأُولى): The wāw is a conjunction and the lām is the lām of inceptive emphasis (lām al-ibtidāʾ), which confirms the content of the sentence. (الْآخِرَةُ) is the mubtadaʾ, (خَيْرٌ) is the khabar, (لَكَ) is attached to (خَيْرٌ), and (مِنَ الْأُولى) is also attached to (خَيْرٌ).
(وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضى): The wāw is a conjunction and the lām is the lām of inception, which also confirms the content of the sentence. The clause (سَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ) is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "you" (anta). It cannot be an oath wāw because that does not enter an imperfect verb except with the nūn of emphasis, so it must be inceptive; and the lām of inception enters only a sentence composed of a mubtadaʾ and khabar, so a mubtadaʾ must be implied and the original must be wa-la-anta sawfa yuʿṭīka rabbuka fa-tarḍā. It is useful to quote for you a question of al-Zamakhsharī and his answer. He said: "If you say: what is the meaning of combining the two particles of emphasis and of postponement? I say: its meaning is that the giving will certainly come about, even if delayed, because of the benefit in the delay." (سَوْفَ) is a particle of the future; (يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ) is an imperfect nominative verb, a fronted object and a postponed agent. The fāʾ is a conjunction, and (تَرْضى) is an imperfect verb conjoined to (يُعْطِيكَ). It is also said that the lām is the lām of oath, and that when a separation occurs between the lām and the verb, the nūn is excluded and the oath lām remains.
(أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيماً فَآوى وَوَجَدَكَ ضَالًّا فَهَدى وَوَجَدَكَ عائِلًا فَأَغْنى): A resumptive passage, set out to enumerate His favours and blessings upon him. The purpose of enumerating them is to strengthen his heart ﷺ and encourage him to keep to the path that Allah chose, which is a path of praiseworthy ends and safe return. The hamza is for confirmatory interrogation; (لَمْ) is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; (يَجِدْكَ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لَمْ), its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "He" (huwa), referring to Allah the Exalted; the kāf is an attached pronoun in the position of accusative, the first direct object; (يَتِيماً) is the second direct object. The fāʾ is a conjunction, and (فَآوى) is conjoined to His saying (أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ), that is, "He found you." It is also possible that wujūd means encountering, not knowing, in which case the kāf is the direct object and (يَتِيماً) is parsed as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the direct object. That is because his father died when he was a foetus, two months before his birth; it is also said, two months after his birth; it is said seven months; it is said nine; it is said twenty-eight months; the first is the well-known one. His mother died when he was four years old; it is said five, six, seven, eight or nine years; it is said twelve years, one month and ten days. His grandfather died when he was eight, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib had entrusted him to Abū Ṭālib, because ʿAbd Allāh and Abū Ṭālib were from the same mother; so Abū Ṭālib was the one who took care of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after his grandfather until Allah sent him as a prophet. (وَوَجَدَكَ) is conjoined, and (ضَالًّا) is the second direct object or a ḥāl. The best that has been said on the meaning of dalāl is that he was devoid of the revealed law, so He guided him by sending it down to him. So by his "straying" is meant his being without a revealed law; it is not meant that he deviated from the truth and wandered in the deserts of error. This meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿ما كُنْتَ تَدْرِي مَا الْكِتابُ وَلَا الْإِيمانُ﴾. There are many other views, too numerous to count, which we have passed over and which can be consulted in the longer works; more on the meaning of dalāl will come in the section on Rhetoric. (وَوَجَدَكَ عائِلًا فَأَغْنى) is conjoined to what preceded and is parsed like it. Al-Farrāʾ said: "His wealth was not from abundance of property, but Allah the Exalted made him content with what He gave him, and that is the reality of wealth." In the hadith: "Wealth is not from abundance of goods, but wealth is the wealth of the soul." And he ﷺ said: "My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear."
(فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلا تَقْهَرْ): The fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa). (أَمَّا) is a particle of condition and detailing. (الْيَتِيمَ) is a direct object fronted before (تَقْهَرْ). The fāʾ links the apodosis. (لا) is prohibitive, and (تَقْهَرْ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لا), its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; that is, do not overpower him regarding his property and so take away his right because of his weakness. This is a lofty teaching, which the Prophet reinforced by his saying: "The best house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is treated well, and the worst house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is treated badly." Then he said, with his two fingers: "I and the guardian of an orphan will be in Paradise like these two."
(وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلا تَنْهَرْ): Conjoined to what precedes. It is preferable that al-sāʾil be taken more generally, whether he asks for money or for knowledge, so that the detailing agrees with and matches the enumeration.
(وَأَمَّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ): Also conjoined. (بِنِعْمَةِ) is attached to (حَدِّثْ). The fāʾ does not prevent this because it is in the position of a redundant one. The favour is wider than to include religion, wealth, shelter, the spoils that came to him and the victory granted to him. Speaking of it is recommended, to stir up resolve and move souls to emulation and imitation. How beautiful is what is reported from him ﷺ, who said: "Allah is beautiful and loves beauty," and He loves to see the trace of His favour upon His servant. It is reported that a man was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, who saw that his clothes were worn, so he ﷺ said to him: "Do you have money?" He said: "Yes." He ﷺ said to him: "When Allah gives you money, let the trace of it be seen on you." And in the hadith also: "A man asked him ﷺ, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, I do good deeds and hide them from people, then it is discovered; do I have a reward in that?' He said: 'You have in that two rewards: the reward of secrecy and the reward of publicity.'"

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying: ﴿وَاللَّيْلِ إِذا سَجى﴾ there is a majāz ʿaqlī (rational figurative attribution), where stillness is attributed to the night. It was stated earlier under majāz ʿaqlī that it is the attribution of a verb, or what has its meaning, to something other than what it belongs to, because of a relation, together with an indication preventing the intended real attribution. Among its finest examples is the saying of Abū al-Ṭayyib in praise of Kāfūr:
أبا المسك أرجو منك نصرا على العدا ... وآمل عزا يخضب البيض بالدم
ويوما يغيظ الحاسدين وحالة ... أقيم الشقا فيها مقام التنعم
(O Abū al-Misk, I hope from you for victory over the enemies, and I look for a glory that dyes the swords with blood; and for a day that enrages the envious, and a state in which I take hardship as a replacement for ease.)
The attribution of dyeing the swords with blood to the pronoun of "glory" is not real, because glory does not dye swords; rather it is the cause of strength and of the gathering of the heroes who dye swords with blood. So the phrase contains a majāz ʿaqlī whose relation is causality. In the verse, the attribution of stillness to the pronoun of the night is not real; what is meant is its people, for they are the ones who become still.
2- In His saying ﴿وَوَجَدَكَ ضَالًّا فَهَدى﴾ there is an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya): the revealed law is likened to guidance, and its absence to straying; the thing likened is omitted and the thing likened to is retained, namely dalāl, from "he went astray (ḍalla) on his road," when he takes a road that does not lead to his destination. The destination here is the beneficial knowledge that elevates mind and spirit together.
3- In His saying ﴿فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلا تَقْهَرْ وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلا تَنْهَرْ﴾ there is the art of iltizām, or lizūm mā lā yalzam (binding oneself to what is not required): the hāʾ is kept constant before the rāʾ. In these two verse-endings, together with the iltizām, there is a wonderful point of subtlety (tankīt). It may be asked: may the two phrases be exchanged, each coming in the place of the other? It is said: that is not permitted, because the point in preferring them as they came is that the orphan is to be disciplined, and the least with which one disciplines is a rebuke (intihār); so he cannot be forbidden to be rebuked. What is forbidden is overpowering him and dominating him, because of his brokenness through orphanhood and the lack of one to help him. From here the coming of each phrase as it came is preferred, and exchanging was not permitted. Some have placed it under the art of takhyīr (choice) among the arts of rhetoric, to which reference was made before.
4- In His saying ﴿وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضى﴾ there is the art of omission (ḥadhf): the second object of (يُعْطِيكَ) is omitted, to magnify the matter and exalt its importance, for these gifts are too great to be mentioned and too large to be listed: that is, the great abundance, from the succession of revelation upon you containing guidance for you and your people, the triumph of your religion, the exaltation of your word, the bringing of happiness to your people through what you legislate for them, and the raising of you and them above the nations in this world and the next.
